Claims about at-least-once/out-of-order object notifications, checksums, object/list consistency and per-object atomicity, immutable manifests/snapshots, atomic metadata swaps, output commits, and success markers match the cited primary sources.

Draft chapter validation accepted all required headings and GitHub-compatible display-math delimiters.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Dataset generation, object version, manifest identity/digest, file role, source interval and consumer receipt have distinct stable meanings.

numerical_recomputation.notes: All explicit file counts, byte totals, digest checks, set differences and receipt behavior reproduce.

evidence: Verified V_M=F_M implies every declared immutable identity is present and no substitute exists in the validated set, while equal cardinality does not imply set equality.
Verified uniqueness condition |{I(f):f in F}|=|F| prevents duplicate manifest identities from inflating totals.
Verified manifest-level idempotence effect(M,effect(M,S))=effect(M,S) is sufficient to absorb duplicate delivery of the same accepted generation.
Verified additive byte/row totals under declared per-entry and row-additivity assumptions.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Set and total properties do not claim semantic row correctness; equality is over exact immutable identities and declared validation scope.

evidence: Reviewed zero/missing/extra/duplicate/truncated/corrupt/version-mismatched files, abandoned multipart uploads, manifest-before-data, quiet-time and listing-count failures.
Reviewed duplicate/out-of-order/delayed/lost notifications, recursive triggers, claim races, lease expiry/fencing and crashes around output, receipt and acknowledgement.
Reviewed path traversal, Unicode/path normalization, symlinks, archive nesting, decompression bombs, schema incompatibility, signature/key failure, sensitive metadata and privacy deletion.
Reviewed corrections, older delayed generation, delete manifests, lifecycle deletion, archive restore, quarantine and source-watermark continuity.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: The ten worked examples and five exercises span producer, storage, notification, parser, consumer, correction and retention boundaries.

evidence: Checked publication-last, unique immutable object identities, stable manifest ID/digest, explicit source/schema scope, exact entry set, size/digest and total reconciliation.
Checked notification independence, fenced claim, all-files-before-publication, durable receipt/output before acknowledgement/watermark, and manifest-level idempotency.
Checked fail-closed authorization/path/schema/compression controls, quarantine without progress, immutable supersession/version order, and referenced-object retention.
invariant_checking.notes: The invariants distinguish discovery from completion, integrity from authentication/semantics, and duplicate delivery from duplicate downstream effect.

evidence: Reviewed exact-set implication and counterexample {a,b} versus {a,c} for count-only validation.
Reviewed publication-last implication conditional on producer conformance and immutable durable object identity.
Reviewed notification-independence from stable manifest retrieval and idempotent conditional receipt.
Reviewed checksum boundary: matching digest supports byte equality under the algorithm but cannot imply authorization, schema validity or source completeness.
proof_review.notes: Proof claims are conditional protocol properties and do not infer multi-object storage transactions or universal cryptographic/semantic correctness.

evidence: Formal statements are labeled theorem, invariant, condition, mechanism or boundary with assumptions adjacent.
Storage-provider behavior is attributed as documented service semantics rather than generalized across filesystems/object stores.
Checksum, notification and listing evidence is explicitly prevented from becoming a stronger semantic-completeness proof.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: The chapter separates deductive set/idempotence results, producer protocol obligations, cryptographic assumptions and empirical validation.

evidence: The executable example is explicitly limited to two known byte strings and an in-memory receipt.
Repeated listings, checksums, totals and restore tests are described as bounded observations with specific blind spots.
Production durability, authentication, parser safety, transactionality, notification recovery and semantic source controls require environment-specific evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: Passing finite file checks is never presented as proof of producer correctness or future arrival completeness.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed the distinctions among arrival, discovery, object identity, producer closure, manifest publication, structural/integrity/schema/semantic validation, notification delivery, claim, receipt, downstream commit, quarantine, correction and retention. The manifest is correctly framed as a logical commit object rather than a transactional file container.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementable producer/consumer state machines, immutable generation keys, publication-last ordering, exact version/length/checksum checks, bounded parsing, notification-plus-poll discovery, fenced claims, stage-validate-publish, receipt/ack ordering, retry, quarantine, supersession, lifecycle and operational monitoring.

pedagogical_review.notes: The one-page review introduces exact-set and idempotence results; exposition follows the boundary from producer through storage/event discovery to consumer publication and repair; notation supports the proofs; the executable fixture gives concrete failures; and ten examples plus five solved exercises cover distinct operational/security reasoning.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed. References and local execution were checked on 2026-09-02. The finite fixture does not establish provider-specific durability, conditional-write behavior, multipart checksum semantics, signature/key trust, parser isolation, producer authorization, source completeness, notification recovery, privacy compliance or production atomicity; those require deployed-system tests and ongoing reconciliation.
